reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Guide specification for drilled shaft construction provided in Appendix D. Adapted primarily from AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications Section 5 (AASHTO, 2017b) with supplementary provisions. Guide specification is NOT intended for direct project application — must be adapted for specific project conditions. Supplementary provisions shown in italics; base AASHTO text in standard font. Additional reference specifications: ACI 336.1-01; ADSC Standards and Specifications for Foundation Drilling Industry (1999); state DOT standard specifications. Chapter provides general discussion of key topics to be addressed in project-specific drilled shaft construction specifications.
key_points: Guide specification in Appendix D based on AASHTO LRFD 2017b Section 5
NOT for direct project use — must be adapted to specific project conditions
Additional references: ACI 336.1-01; ADSC 1999; state DOT specifications
Commentary in Appendix D assists engineers in adapting to project-specific conditions
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft construction specifications on transportation projects

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.body: Drilled shaft performance is highly dependent on construction means and methods. Key performance-construction relationships: poor bottom cleaning reduces base resistance; prolonged slurry exposure reduces side resistance; unstable excavation causes voids or soil inclusions compromising structural integrity. Unlike driven piles (where driving resistance indicates performance), drilled shaft performance verification relies on consistent and repeatable application of installation procedures demonstrated by successful technique and test shafts. Specification must emphasize: qualified contractor and key personnel; Drilled Shaft Installation Plan preparation and review; appropriate installation methods for ground/groundwater conditions; technique shafts to evaluate contractor's means and methods; load test shafts to verify design assumptions; integrity testing per Chapter 16; clearly defined acceptance criteria and tolerances.
key_points: Performance is highly dependent on construction means and methods
Poor bottom cleaning reduces base resistance; prolonged slurry exposure reduces side resistance
Specification must require Installation Plan, technique shafts, qualified contractor
Drilled shaft performance cannot be verified by a single direct indicator like driving resistance
sections.applicability: Specification development for drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Qualifications of Drilled Shaft Contractors
sections.body: Drilled shafts are frequently high-capacity, non-redundant elements requiring high-quality workmanship achievable only by experienced contractors. Specifications must require minimum contractor qualifications. Require successful installation of technique shaft(s) at start of construction to demonstrate capabilities. Establish minimum qualifications for key contractor staff: superintendent, foremen, lead drillers, testing personnel, independent inspectors (design-build). Avoid splitting drilled shaft work: general contractor should not hire specialty contractor for excavation only while assigning steel/concrete to different organization — increases coordination effort, delays concrete placement, invites disputes over shaft defects. All critical operations (excavation, steel, concrete) must be performed in continuous, coordinated manner by single qualified contractor.
key_points: Require minimum contractor qualifications for drilled shaft specialty work
Require technique shaft(s) at start of construction to demonstrate contractor's methods
Key personnel qualification requirements: superintendent, foremen, lead drillers
Avoid splitting excavation/steel/concrete work between separate subcontractors — invites disputes

sections.title: Construction Method
sections.body: Permitted construction methods must consider ground and groundwater conditions and design requirements (side resistance, base resistance, or combined). Factors influenced: drilling equipment type, excavation method (wet or dry), drilling fluid type, casing (permanent or temporary), shaft cleanout criteria, concrete mix design and placement method. For wet excavations: specify concrete slump/spread range, minimum workability duration, and maximum aggregate size for tremie placement. Specification must not needlessly restrict contractor choice of tools, equipment, or method — flexibility maximizes cost effectiveness. However, when site conditions clearly dictate certain methods (e.g., wet methods below groundwater in cohesionless soils), general requirements are appropriate.
key_points: Permit as much contractor flexibility as possible within project and site constraints
Specify slump/spread, workability retention, and max aggregate size for wet excavation concrete
Dictate installation method only when site conditions clearly require it (e.g., wet method in sands below GWT)
Construction method influences both resistance and structural integrity of completed shaft
sections.applicability: Construction method specification; contractor flexibility provisions

sections.title: Drilling Fluid
sections.body: Drilling fluid specification must address type permitted (mineral slurry, polymer slurry, or water) appropriate for ground conditions and installation method. Primary concerns in slurry use: borehole stability maintained during excavation and concrete placement; slurry does not weaken concrete/soil or concrete/steel bond; all slurry displaced from excavation by rising concrete; sediment not deposited in excavation or rising concrete. Specification provisions for drilling fluid: identify permitted fluid types; specify slurry property ranges during excavation and prior to concrete placement (Marsh Funnel viscosity, density, pH, sand content); require slurry inspection testing; require pre-production technique shaft(s) to evaluate wet excavation method. Bentonite: Marsh Funnel 28-40 sec, density ≤1.15 g/cm³, pH 7.5-11, sand ≤4%. Polymer: Marsh Funnel 34-80 sec, density ≤1.01 g/cm³, pH 7-12, sand ≤1%.
key_points: Four primary concerns: stability, no bond reduction, full displacement by concrete, no sediment deposition
Bentonite QC limits: Marsh Funnel 28-40 sec, density ≤1.15 g/cm³, pH 7.5-11, sand ≤4%
Polymer QC limits: Marsh Funnel 34-80 sec, density ≤1.01 g/cm³, pH 7-12, sand ≤1%
Technique shaft required to evaluate wet excavation method before production
sections.applicability: Drilling fluid specification for wet construction

sections.title: Load Testing
sections.body: Load testing specified for projects requiring high capacity foundations, where geotechnical resistance cannot be reliably estimated, or where shaft count justifies cost. Conventional static load tests (kentledge/reaction frame) generally impractical for high-capacity drilled shafts. Bi-directional load cell testing is most practical and economical for high-capacity shafts — per ASTM D8169/D8169M. Rapid compression force pulse (Statnamic) per ASTM D7383. High strain dynamic testing per ASTM D4945. Specification must include: test shaft construction requirements matching production shafts; instrumentation plan; test procedures and acceptance criteria; interpretation requirements; provisions for incorporating test results into production design.
key_points: Specify load testing for high capacity projects or when resistance cannot be reliably estimated
Bi-directional (O-cell): ASTM D8169/D8169M — most practical for high capacity shafts
Rapid force pulse (Statnamic): ASTM D7383
High strain dynamic: ASTM D4945
Test shaft construction must match production shaft procedures
sections.applicability: Load test specification; load test program requirements in contract documents

sections.title: Other Specification Topics
sections.body: Drilled Shaft Installation Plan (DSIP): contractor-prepared document submitted and approved before construction; required content includes: proposed equipment and tools; installation methods for each stratum; casing plan; drilling fluid plan; concrete mix design; concrete placement procedures; contingency plan for unexpected conditions. Technique shafts: demonstrate contractor's capabilities in project-specific conditions; require construction log and inspection; perform integrity test; perform load test if appropriate; may precede production by days-weeks on complex sites. Concrete: specify minimum slump/spread, workability retention, maximum aggregate size, minimum f'c; prohibit addition of water at jobsite; volume monitoring requirements. Concrete placement: require volume monitoring and recording; establish acceptable volume tolerance. Acceptance criteria and tolerances: location (plan position, ±3 in. for shaft centers); alignment (vertical to ≤1/4 in. per 10 ft = 2% grade); top of shaft elevation; concrete cutoff elevation. Records: require complete drilled shaft installation records per Chapter 15 checklist. Integrity testing requirements per Chapter 16 (CSL, TIP, or other methods).
key_points: Drilled Shaft Installation Plan (DSIP): contractor-prepared, submitted for approval before construction
DSIP content: equipment, methods, casing plan, slurry plan, concrete mix, placement procedures, contingency
Technique shafts: demonstrate contractor capabilities; may require load test and integrity test
Concrete addition of water at jobsite: PROHIBIT
Alignment tolerance: ≤1/4 in. per 10 ft (2% grade) or ≤1 in./10 ft for typical transportation projects
Require complete installation records per Chapter 15
sections.applicability: Drilled Shaft Installation Plan; technique shafts; acceptance tolerances

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter discussed key topics for drilled shaft construction specifications: contractor qualifications, construction methods, drilling fluid requirements, load testing, Installation Plan requirements, technique shafts, concrete requirements, acceptance criteria, records, and integrity testing. Guide specification in Appendix D (based on AASHTO 2017b Section 5) provides a starting point. Specifications must be adapted to site-specific conditions and project requirements.
